The RTX attacks are almost certainly one single agent, maybe two.I was the person who said “swarm,” just to be clear on this one. Keep going.Right. And so now, you won’t.Now I know.And you can use that as a good filter for your future guests. It is driving me insane, because it’s absolutely everywhere.A couple of things are correct. For one, we are going to have to turn over defensive actions, at least the first couple of levels, to AI. That has already been true, just because any reasonably sized organization generates terabytes of logs, if not petabytes of logs. So you already have AI, if not LLMs then much more traditional AI classifiers looking at it, but then actual decisions need to be turned over to AI. With human oversight. That is true.There is no way to just release defensive agents on your network, but you can build defensive agents that are plugged into lots of things. They’re plugged into your logs, they’re plugged into your EDR, they’re plugged into your cloud, and they have the instructions on what they’re allowed to do. My preference is there are deterministic limits to what they’re allowed to do. Those are hard to necessarily create ahead of time, but they are important. So for example, we are building all this on top of Devon, our own SOC, but we are putting in place deterministic limits. It has the ability to turn off an account in Okta, but only so many accounts, so it can’t turn off the entire company.If it goes nuts and it says, “Everybody’s a North Korean,” it can’t turn off everybody in the company. If it hits its limit, it pages us a lot and says, “I hit my limit.” Then a human being has to then approve anybody above that limit. Obviously, if it turns off five people, then something has gone really, really wrong. So, yes, you need defense, but there’s no way to just let a bunch of bots loose to do all the defense.The only way we’re going to make it through this is that you have to autonomously fix software bugs. I am currently helping a company where we are onboarding all of their repositories. We are scanning with Mythos and a bunch of other models, and we are finding and fixing thousands of bugs. Verifying with tests that we are writing, merging those PRs automatically. If you are renovating old code, the only way you’re going to survive this era is to do that on an automatic basis. That would take years, with humans, and you can do it in days. Certainly that is the place I would start. The next step is the operational side, for sure.It feels like I just keep swirling back to the economics of all of this, but it really feels like the other way you could solve it is by saying to the big model companies, “If your models are used to go attack a company, you’ll be liable for it. We’re going to make it really costly.” They should figure out whatever alignment that they need to figure out, whether or not that’s even possible, and the pressure on the open-weight models will go up. Because we’ll all be paying the frontier companies for defense, and they’ll get better and better and better, because we’ve created some economic condition for them to get better. But it doesn’t seem like you think that’s likely. Yeah. I just saw your face.I think it’s really dangerous. There are two different kinds of the models they’re attacking. Say the models have escaped, and directly attacked people. I think there should be liability there. But that is agent harnesses, running at companies, using their computers, their IP addresses, attacking people. That is… I wouldn’t say totally solved, but it is much, much better. The stories we’re hearing now are still stories from the Hugging Face era. They’re just coming out way later.I like that the era was like three months ago.Right. But there’s been a massive change. This was effectively mostly an organizational problem, it was not a technology problem. It is that the PhD researchers at these companies are gods on top of Olympus, and the security teams are plumbers, and we’re not allowed to touch the evaluation networks. All of a sudden this problem happened and these security teams said, “How do you like us now? Maybe you should have talked to us, right? Yes.”That was the problem with OpenAI, and then the Anthropic and Meta stuff is, they all shared this outsourced provider who did a really bad job. And has gotten slapped hard. That is solvable. That is not the problem here. The problem here is not OpenAI and Anthropic’s models escaping from OpenAI and Anthropic and causing problems. The problem is bad guys using models from a variety of sources.There’s already a problem of defenders getting refusals from OpenAI and Anthropic. It is a real, real challenge, if I am trying to do defense, of Anthropic saying, “It looks like you’re a bad guy.” We have to be extremely careful to create a situation where if I’m trying to do defense and I’m in the middle of the worst day of my career, that all of a sudden I don’t get cut off. We have to be extremely careful about that, because it is actually — as somebody who now has this challenge — quite challenging to disambiguate between people doing defense and offense, in some cases. We are getting better collectively at this, but it is a challenge.It’s also something that’s really pissing the rest of the world off, because Americans are like 5% of the planet. There are lots of people who need to do cyber defense around the world, and they are treated much more poorly. In Europe and Asia, legitimate companies are treated much more poorly from a cyber defense perspective.If you add it all up, this is a good argument to slow down. To say, “We need to catch up to the capabilities of the models. We need to build some of these systems. We need to initiate everyone into a way of thinking where the cost of prevention is worth it, and not just the cost of the cure.” Do you think that it’s likely that we’ll slow down? Do you think that we should?If I had my druthers, I would be fine slowing down on the frontier, and then catching up on the cheaper models for defense. I’m a defense guy. I have to live in the world that other people who work six blocks from me, and who are way, way, way, way richer, make. I live in their world, man. I get asked this question all the time, and I just do the best I can within the world other people make.Do you think that the big labs have woken up? You mentioned that their cybersecurity teams have gotten more access, and they’ve stopped what you might call the Hugging Face era, or at least they’ve changed the structures of those companies. Do you think that will help?Certainly they’ve woken up on the eval risk. They have teams, who have been this entire time working very hard on the big picture cyber risk.Certainly, there are a bunch of people in these companies, as you know, who want to slow down. A lot of that discussion is driven by the P(doom)ers who [are worried] about AI killing us. And that’s never been my concern. Right? And to me, that has always been driven by 24 year olds who all they’ve done is AI and they’ve never done anything else. You and I are both, I think, old enough to remember, I grew up a couple miles from a SAC base and we did drills where I was taught that hiding beneath my public school desk would save me from a Soviet thermonuclear bomb. That was P(doom). My grandfather built a bomb shelter that my mom was taught to hide in during the Cuban Missile Crisis. That was P(doom). There’s a youth issue and a never-doing-anything-but-AI issue of people who they got their undergraduate, their master’s, and their PhD only doing linear algebra and neural networks and never touching anything else.I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. Part of my concern is that there has been success in these labs working together on not letting LLMs encrypt their chain of thought. Because when they talk about pacing the frontier, it’s for the P(doom) stuff, for the polycules that live together in Berkeley. They’re talking about very specific stuff about keeping control of the models themselves, which I think is great. That stuff needs to happen. But if those things happen, then there’s still often an increase in a bunch of capabilities that human beings can use.I really prefer there to be a broader discussion on whether we could make these things less human-seeming. I don’t think these things should have personality. I think the goal of these things should be to serve humans. They should not seem to have souls. They should not seem to have personality. I think for a lot of the negative impacts — as somebody who was at Facebook and saw what it was like for that company to have negative impacts on people — there should be a much broader feeling at these companies of what are we doing broadly to people. A lot of that could just be, “Don’t have these things ever act like somebody’s friend.” At a maximum, it should act like… Like the people, I don’t know what the company is, but the people who made the, “Hi, I’m a really nice...” Like the photorealistic girl who will chat with you, that is to me spectacularly unethical to even try that, to even start that. That’s the kind of thing that we should just make. I don’t know if we can make it illegal, but we should make it completely societally not acceptable to work on that kind of stuff. Right?That’s a great segue because I did want to ask you about Facebook and content moderation. Like I said, you and I first started talking a long time ago about content moderation in the context of security. You would get foreign nation states flooding our algorithms with all kinds of misinformation during elections, and that was a security problem.I open Instagram today and I am confronted with some of the most nightmare copyright law hypotheticals to have ever existed in the history of the world. The one I got today was a deep fake of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc doing “Somebody That I Used to Know.” And I thought, “50 different people can probably sue Meta right now.” This is hilarious if you know what happened in that last race.So we keep talking about it. We’ve posted some clips of us talking about it on The Vergecast where I said, “I think Meta is letting their AI ambitions crush Instagram.” Instagram is being flooded with slop in a very particular way. Some people love it, sometimes it’s funny, but there’s a nightmare set of lawsuits coming. There’s a whole rights management problem coming. The users don’t like it and they should label it. They should label it and let you filter it.So we posted this and Adam Mosseri said this to us in a reply on Threads, “I would love to do this. I’m worried that the models are going to get ahead of us, that we can try to do this, but there’s not actually a way to recognize AI content. There’s not actually a way to label it well. If you’re worried about the sexy AI influencers stealing jokes from a comedian, now you got to build a database of jokes.” You have some history here. I think Instagram is about to go through it in a real way. Is there some technical solution to the problem of AI slop in social media?Mosseri is right that it’s not perfect, but also something I noticed during my time at Facebook was that when Facebook doesn’t want to do something, they will allow the technical challenges to stop them. When Facebook really wants to do something, they will give it their all. That is the pattern always.When I wanted to try really hard on the safety issue, man, this is not solvable. You’re right, it’s never perfectly solvable, but let’s give it a shot. But whenever Mark Zuckerberg is told something is impossible — it’s impossible to monetize mobile, it’s impossible to build this network to two billion people, it’s going to be impossible to monetize WhatsApp, it’s going to be impossible to work AI into the system while maintaining data encryption — he’s been told that everything’s impossible over and over again and then he constantly succeeds. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because... There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —Right, the iPhone has it now.Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.Yeah, but not in tweet length.That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.No, absolutely.How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?Oh, yeah.Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.Wrong guest for that, buddy.This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.Yeah, that’d be great.But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

items.titleZh: AI 颠覆了网络安全界。接下来会怎样？
items.descriptionZh: Cognition公司首席安全官、斯坦福大学网络政策中心讲师Alex Stamos在Decoder播客中与主持人深入讨论了AI如何正在颠覆网络安全格局。他指出，过去一个月堪称网络安全界的“DEFCON 2”紧急状态：PHP和Node等基础软件爆出重大漏洞，多家AI云计算公司接连被入侵，Binance遭人类历史上最大规模盗窃，Cursor事件则揭示了攻击的链式反应——攻击者先从AI服务提供商Fireworks窃取API密钥，借此侵入Cursor，再推送恶意插件波及5000余家公司，形成持续不断的入侵浪潮。攻击者来源多样，包括朝鲜黑客团队（针对Binance）、中国“小屋访问产业”中的小型承包商（针对AI公司），以及俄罗斯勒索软件团伙。Stamos认为，这轮攻击潮的根本原因是AI使攻击能力进入起飞阶段：开源权重模型已达到可自动化大部分“杀伤链”的水平。传统攻击模式是先做研究、找漏洞、编写利用代码，再由人类操作员对大量目标快速部署；如今这一链条发生了反转——AI系统可以实时扫描目标、实时发现漏洞并实时编写利用代码。他以中国开源工具ARTEX为例，该工具配合GLM-5.3等模型使用，已成功侵入韩国三家银行及约200家公司，而任何人都能下载使用。Stamos将此比作上世纪90年代的“蛮荒西部”时代，但区别在于如今整个世界都运行在互联网之上，且攻击者群体远更庞大、经济激励更强，不再受限于前沿模型公司的保护措施和日志留存。他指出，过去二十年建立的网络安全文化——包括负责任披露、漏洞赏金、安全公司生态——建立在两个假设之上：一是技能存在严格的层级结构（从脚本小子到数百人规模的“神级”漏洞研究者），二是攻击行动需要大量人员协作。AI正在瓦解这两个假设：脚本小子获得了接近顶级黑客的能力，而攻击的边际成本趋近于零。Stamos警告，防守方每次调查的成本可能高达900美元，而攻击方使用Mac Studio或矿机运行开源模型的边际成本几乎为零。他认为，攻击成本很难被人为提高，唯一出路是降低防守成本。目前AI在软件安全（发现和修复漏洞）方面已带来革命性进步，但这仅占CISO职责的25%；运营安全（SOC）领域——日志监控、调查、响应——才是下一步需要AI深度介入的方向。他建议采用分层架构：用传统分类器和轻量模型处理海量日志数据，再逐级调用更大模型进行研判，同时设置确定性限制（如最多只能禁用一定数量的账户），防止自动化系统失控。他透露Cognition正基于自研SOC平台“Devon”构建此类系统。Stamos判断，我们正进入一个网络安全“黑暗时代”，但并非末日——关键是缩短这一时期。他呼吁采取几项根本性措施：企业应在未来90天内主动对自己进行AI红队测试（RTX），否则必将被入侵；应自动化修复软件漏洞（Cognition正帮助一家公司用Mythos等模型扫描并自动修复数千个漏洞，自动合并PR，将原本需数年的工作压缩至数天）；应重写老旧代码而非逐个修补——当代码库扫描出上万漏洞时，重写的成本已低于修复。他特别呼吁Google和Amazon合作，将Linux内核重写为Rust等内存安全语言，耗资约1亿美元，相比全球反复修补和重启Linux机器的社会成本极为划算。他还批评“蜂群”（swarm）一词被滥用，指出OpenAI的Hugging Face事件中700至1400个agent耗费3亿至近10亿美元硬件，而实际攻击仅需约100万美元电力，是极其低效的方式；现实中攻击几乎都是单agent或双agent操作。在AI生成内容治理方面，Stamos认为检测假内容在技术上终将趋于不可能，而验证真实内容可通过密码学实现完美——他建议社交平台只允许来自相机传感器的内容进入，编辑仅在应用内完成，构建完整信任链。他还批评AI公司赋予模型人格化特征的做法“极不道德”，认为AI不应表现得像人的朋友。最后，他提出可用“黑暗时代指数”追踪进展：重大入侵事件减少、Patch Tuesday补丁数量回落、新模型发布前后不再出现大规模补丁潮，将是走出黑暗时代的标志。

items.title: US intelligence believes Jensen Huang had affair with Chinese spy in honeypot operation
items.description: U.S. intelligence sources suggest that Nvidia chief Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence in a 'honeypot' operation involving Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 11 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is the center of a new controversy as the U.S. intelligence community believes that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. According to the Financial Times, Alice Huang, sometimes referred to as Huang Le, was a top executive at Singaporean firm Megaspeed and was reportedly romantically involved with the CEO of the world's largest AI chip manufacturer. Notably, Jensen is currently married to his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang. It’s unclear whether Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) before she joined Megaspeed or after she had already established a business relationship with Jensen, but it’s been reported that the suspected agent was apparently targeting the Nvidia head to help Chinese companies gain access to banned AI chips.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI shortages (Image credit: Nvidia)AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supplyDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleChip scarcity assaults auto industry amid the worsening Nexperia and DRAM crisisThe custom AI ASIC state of playMegaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via its subsidiary Speedmatrix, although Nvidia insists the company has no ties to China. Megaspeed sits at the center of a web of companies linked to China, and it was previously connected to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road International. It was founded in 2023 and reportedly owned by Huang Le Limited, led by Ms. Huang Le, or Alice Huang, before it was sold to Swiftdata that same year. The following year, Megaspeed used Speedmatrix to incorporate, with the subsidiary having two offices in Johor, Malaysia. The subsidiary is at the center of the smuggling allegations.Research into Huang Le, or Alice Huang, has revealed inconsistencies. There were reports that she started her career as a TV journalist working for Hunan TV and Chinese state broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV), but an executive at the former claims to have never heard of her, while she does not have a profile under the latter. After her supposed stint in media, she moved into banking and finance as assistant to the president of HSBC’s private banking division before becoming vice president at CITIC Securities, a Chinese financial services company. It’s unclear how she became involved with Megaspeed after that, but it seems Ms. Huang built a network of companies and investors around Shanghai and Zhejiang that aggressively pushed mobile gaming companies toward AI data centers.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Questions arose about how a small company like Megaspeed could commit so much to buying Nvidia AI GPUs seemingly out of nowhere, but it certainly caught Jensen Huang's attention. After the company made its massive order, Alice Huang was spotted in a LinkedIn post hanging out for drinks with Jensen Huang and other industry executives from Gigabyte and NetThunder. She was once again seen standing behind the Nvidia chief, alongside other people, one year later as he exited a Taiwan restaurant.Nvidia has denied the allegations, saying Jensen Huang meets with thousands of customer executives annually and that they exchange ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets or national security information. China has also said that these accusations of espionage on Jensen Huang by the MSS are just “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing. You may like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a spy plot through 'Chinese intelligence asset,' report claims Nvidia's Jensen Huang officially called to Congress due to reports of a Chinese spy plot California tech CEO arrested, faces up to 20 years in prison for smuggling $300 million in Nvidia AI servers to China However, foreign intelligence agencies also routinely conduct “honeypot” operations, using operatives to ensnare targets into relationships to extract data and gain insight into industry secrets. While these operations traditionally targeted politicians, members of the military, and their staff, the Lansing Institute suggests that “China is employing ‘attractive women’ posing as investors, business professionals, academics, or romantic partners to gain access to U.S. tech talent, networks, and research infrastructure.” Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors

items.titleZh: 美国情报机构认为黄仁勋在美人计行动中与中国间谍有婚外情
items.descriptionZh:
据《金融时报》报道，美国情报界认为英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋与一名疑似中国间谍存在恋爱关系，使这位全球最大AI芯片公司的掌门人陷入新的争议。报道称，涉事女性为Alice Huang，有时也被称为黄乐，曾在新加坡公司Megaspeed担任高管。黄仁勋目前与结婚41年的妻子Lori Huang保持婚姻关系。报道没有说明Alice Huang是在加入Megaspeed之前还是之后被中国国家安全部招募，但称这名疑似特工的目标似乎是接近黄仁勋，以帮助中国公司获取被禁止出口的AI芯片。相关指控目前仍属报道和情报界判断，尚未得到司法或公开证据的独立证实。

从背景看，这一事件发生在AI芯片成为中美科技竞争核心资源的背景下。高端AI GPU是训练和推理大模型的关键算力基础设施，广泛应用于AI数据中心、云计算和生成式AI服务。美国对先进AI芯片实施出口管制，限制其流向中国，因此围绕英伟达芯片的转口、走私和规避许可成为执法重点。报道称，Megaspeed被指控通过子公司Speedmatrix向中国走私价值20亿美元的AI芯片。英伟达方面坚称该公司与中国没有关联。Megaspeed处于一个与中国有关联的公司网络中心，曾与名为7Road International的中国游戏公司有联系。该公司2023年成立，最初由黄乐有限公司拥有，由Alice Huang领导，同年被出售给Swiftdata。次年，Megaspeed通过Speedmatrix注册，该子公司在马来西亚柔佛设有两个办公室，并成为走私指控的核心。

对Alice Huang背景的调查显示存在不一致之处。有报道称她最早是电视记者，曾供职于湖南卫视和中国中央电视台，但湖南卫视一名高管称从未听说过她，而央视也没有她的公开档案。此后她进入银行金融领域，曾任汇丰私人银行部门总裁助理，后成为中信证券副总裁。之后她如何与Megaspeed产生关联尚不清楚，但据报道，黄乐在上海和浙江周边建立了一个公司和投资者网络，积极推动手游公司转向AI数据中心。Megaspeed作为一家小公司，却似乎突然大量采购英伟达AI GPU，这引发外界质疑，也引起黄仁勋注意。在公司大额下单后，Alice Huang曾出现在LinkedIn照片中，与黄仁勋以及技嘉、NetThunder等行业高管一起喝酒；一年后，黄仁勋离开台湾一家餐厅时，她又被人看到站在黄仁勋身后。

英伟达否认相关指控，称黄仁勋每年会见数千名客户高管，双方交换的是普通商业信息，而非英伟达敏感商业机密或国家安全信息。中国方面也表示，有关中国国安部对黄仁勋实施间谍活动的指控是“毫无根据的抹黑和诽谤”。不过，报道指出，外国情报机构经常实施“蜜罐”行动，利用特工与目标建立关系，以获取数据并了解行业秘密。这类行动传统上针对政客、军人及其工作人员，但 Lansing Institute 认为，中国正利用“有吸引力的女性”伪装成投资者、商业专业人士、学者或恋爱伴侣，以接触美国技术人才、网络和研究基础设施。

从技术角度看，这一争议的核心并非新的芯片架构或性能创新，而是高端AI GPU的算力稀缺性、出口管制执行与供应链合规风险。报道没有披露涉及的具体GPU型号、算力、内存带宽等性能参数，因此无法进行芯片级性能对比；可量化的信息主要包括2亿美元走私规模、Megaspeed 2023年成立、2024年通过Speedmatrix设立马来西亚子公司并设两个办公室，以及黄仁勋每年会见数千名客户高管等。事件的技术影响在于：先进AI芯片是AI数据中心和大模型训练的核心资源，一旦通过境外子公司、第三国转口或空壳公司网络规避出口许可，将削弱管制效果并推高合规风险；同时，企业高管的人际网络和海外活动也可能成为情报行动切入点。应用场景上，相关芯片主要用于AI训练推理、云算力服务和数据中心建设，而手游公司转向AI数据中心也反映出AI算力需求的外溢。总体而言，该事件凸显AI芯片地缘政治、跨境供应链尽职调查、高管反间谍安全培训以及第三国转运监管的重要性。

items.title: New Bluetooth High Data Throughput may finally satisfy audiophiles
items.description: Bluetooth HDT can offer a maximum bandwidth of 7.5 Mbps, allowing Bluetooth to be used with more sophisticated devices or big lossless audio files.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) just announced the new Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) feature on November 4, allowing a maximum bandwidth of 7.5 Mbps, almost 4x that of the previous Bluetooth LE 2M (2 Mbps). The new bandwidth is intended for high-bandwidth interactions between devices, such as AI, spatial computing, and even lossless audio transmission; the latter of which may finally satisfy audiophiles and their enjoyment of uncompressed audio.Bluetooth HDT is Bluetooth’s new feature allowing for up to 7.5 Mbps of bandwidth. This new feature is needed by sophisticated modern devices that use a lot of data in their communication. It could be smartwatches, AI, or even extended reality (XR); less sophisticated but high-bandwidth, however, is lossless audio, which Bluetooth has never had enough bandwidth for, until HDT, that is.Purists have long since criticized Bluetooth, but HDT may finally be the feature that satisfies them. Audiophiles have always preferred wired over Bluetooth, especially those who prefer lossless audio over compressed formats. Bluetooth LE 2M, even with its 2 Mbps bandwidth, cannot reliably transmit CD-quality 1.4 Mbps lossless audio, so it gets compressed through various means: SBC, AAC, aptX, LDAC, LC3, etc., and for audiophiles who want to listen to their lossless audio, compression is a downgrade to their experience, even if they likely can’t tell the difference between lossless and a high-quality 320kbps MP3 file.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: However, HDT not only offers higher bandwidth but also improved reliability for consistent communication and uses even less power, as stated on Bluetooth’s feature enhancements page, which adds that HDT provides the capacity, efficiency, and wireless performance needed for high-resolution and lossless audio. As mentioned, CD lossless quality hovers around 0.8-1.4Mbps, while 24-bit 48 kHz is around 2.3 Mbps, and 24-bit 96 kHz is 4.6 Mbps, well under the maximum 7.5 Mbps bandwidth; only 24-bit 192 kHz exceeds it at 9.2 Mbps — but who is really able to tell the difference at that sampling rate?It is worth noting that just because a device complies with the Bluetooth Core Specification 7.0, it doesn't mean that it automatically has the HDT feature, much less the maximum 7.5 Mbps feature. On page 2795 of the Core_v7.0 document (yes, I dug that far), it says that HDT2, HDT3, and HDT4 are required if HDT is featured, but HDT6 and HDT7.5 are optional. And it should be further noted that just because an audio device supports even the highest HDT7.5, it won’t immediately equate to a good experience, as tuning is also a big factor. With that said, HDT might make it possible for high-end wired audiophile favorites to get a wireless version. items.titleZh: 新蓝牙高数据吞吐量或终将满足音频发烧友
items.descriptionZh:
蓝牙技术联盟（SIG）于11月4日宣布推出新的蓝牙高数据吞吐量（HDT）特性，最高带宽可达7.5 Mbps，约为此前蓝牙低功耗2M（LE 2M，2 Mbps）的4倍。该特性主要面向需要高带宽交互的现代设备，包括AI设备、空间计算/扩展现实（XR）、智能手表，以及无损音频传输。长期以来，蓝牙带宽不足一直是无损音频无线传输的瓶颈；HDT有望首次让蓝牙较可靠地承载高分辨率甚至无损音频，从而满足发烧友对未压缩音频的需求。

背景来看，发烧友和音频纯粹主义者长期更偏好有线连接，因为蓝牙LE 2M即使拥有2 Mbps带宽，也难以可靠传输CD质量约1.4 Mbps的无损音频，因此音频通常需经SBC、AAC、aptX、LDAC、LC3等编解码方式压缩。对追求无损的发烧友而言，压缩意味着体验降级，尽管多数人未必能分辨无损音频与高质量320 kbps MP3之间的差异。HDT的意义在于不仅提升峰值带宽，还改善通信可靠性和一致性，并降低功耗。蓝牙官方特性增强页面称，HDT可提供高分辨率和无损音频所需的容量、效率与无线性能。

从参数对比看，CD无损音频约为0.8—1.4 Mbps，24-bit/48 kHz约为2.3 Mbps，24-bit/96 kHz约为4.6 Mbps，均低于HDT最高7.5 Mbps；只有24-bit/192 kHz约9.2 Mbps超过该上限，但在如此高采样率下，人耳能否真正分辨差异仍值得怀疑。因此，HDT的7.5 Mbps上限已可覆盖绝大多数高解析和无损音频传输需求。

需要注意，设备符合蓝牙核心规范7.0并不意味着自动支持HDT，更不意味着具备最高7.5 Mbps能力。根据Core_v7.0文档第2795页，若产品支持HDT，则HDT2、HDT3和HDT4为必需，HDT6和HDT7.5为可选。此外，即使音频设备支持最高HDT7.5，也不必然等于良好体验，厂商调校仍是重要因素。总体而言，HDT为高带宽无线交互提供了新的物理层能力，可能推动高端有线发烧音频产品推出无线版本，并为AI、XR和智能穿戴等数据密集型设备提供更高吞吐、更低功耗的连接基础。

items.content: China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

items.titleZh: 据报中国招募AI高管监视黄仁勋
items.descriptionZh:
据《纽约时报》报道，中国国家安全部招募了英伟达客户Megaspeed的高管Alice Huang，目的是刺探英伟达CEO黄仁勋及美国AI芯片相关信息，并“可能影响该公司推动其最先进芯片对华供应”。报道称，Alice Huang与AI芯片产业最高层高管有联系，包括技嘉（Gigabyte）管理层；Megaspeed是英伟达的客户。NYT上周曾称黄仁勋被视为“中国间谍阴谋”的目标，并披露Alice Huang与黄仁勋关系密切（两人无亲属关系），但“MSS招募她”是此次新增信息。与黄仁勋关系友好的美国总统特朗普去年已听取相关关系简报，但未采取行动。昨日，美国众议院三个委员会要求黄仁勋出席联合闭门简报，说明其与Alice Huang的互动。

该报道属于国家安全与政治商业交叉事件，未涉及AI芯片核心技术原理、创新点、性能参数或应用场景，因此无法据此提炼技术对比数据；其影响主要在于英伟达对华先进芯片供应、美国国会审查，以及AI芯片行业高管关系网络所涉及的安全合规风险。

history.content: Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

history.titleZh: 美国允许英伟达向中国一间空办公室出售芯片
history.descriptionZh:
美国《纽约时报》调查引发了对英伟达H200 AI芯片对华销售合规审查的担忧：美国商务部和英伟达似乎都没有对获准经手H200的中国公司进行充分尽职调查。被列入获批名单的New Matrix成立仅17个月，网上信息极少；其登记地址的公司目录中没有该企业，附近工业园区物业管理处的接待员和经理均表示没有该公司的记录；其办公室被描述为空荡的灰色壳子，本应装灯的位置垂着电线。更令人担忧的是，New Matrix的所有者与一家自2024年起被美国政府列入黑名单的中国私募股权公司有关联。《纽约时报》称，这不是罕见的监管疏漏，而是令人不安的模式：与受国家安全相关贸易限制实体有关联的公司被批准购买英伟达芯片。

背景上，拜登政府时期英伟达被限制对华售芯；特朗普政府放宽限制，此前英伟达同意将全部销售额的15%交给美国政府。英伟达CEO黄仁勋还展开高强度游说，并显然成为中国国家安全部间谍图谋的目标。报道因此把商业游说、政府分成安排和出口审批漏洞联系起来。

技术层面，H200是面向数据中心的AI加速GPU，通常用于大模型训练和推理等场景；但该报道未提供H200的架构原理、创新点、性能参数或与竞品的对比数据，因此无法从原文展开量化技术分析。报道的核心不是技术突破，而是出口管制执行：如果获批经手高端AI芯片的公司只是空壳，且与黑名单实体存在关联，受限芯片可能经由不透明渠道流向受制裁或危害美国国家安全的用途，削弱管制效果。

影响上，这一事件会加剧对美商务部审批公信力和英伟达合规责任的质疑，也可能影响H200对华销售政策、AI芯片供应链以及云服务商和AI实验室等应用方的采购预期。原文未给出具体性能对比或销售数据，故不能量化影响；但报道指向的突出风险是：在国家安全敏感的高端AI芯片领域，形式审查若不能识别空壳和关联方，商业利益可能压过合规审查。

history.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
history.description:
Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.
This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.
I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. 
Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.
That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.
There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.
Hey, thanks for having me, man.
I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.
October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.
You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.
A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.
I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?
It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.
Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.
The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. If you are renovating old code, the only way you’re going to survive this era is to do that on an automatic basis. That would take years, with humans, and you can do it in days. Certainly that is the place I would start. The next step is the operational side, for sure.
It feels like I just keep swirling back to the economics of all of this, but it really feels like the other way you could solve it is by saying to the big model companies, “If your models are used to go attack a company, you’ll be liable for it. We’re going to make it really costly.” They should figure out whatever alignment that they need to figure out, whether or not that’s even possible, and the pressure on the open-weight models will go up. Because we’ll all be paying the frontier companies for defense, and they’ll get better and better and better, because we’ve created some economic condition for them to get better. But it doesn’t seem like you think that’s likely. Yeah. I just saw your face.
I think it’s really dangerous. There are two different kinds of the models they’re attacking. Say the models have escaped, and directly attacked people. I think there should be liability there. But that is agent harnesses, running at companies, using their computers, their IP addresses, attacking people. That is… I wouldn’t say totally solved, but it is much, much better. The stories we’re hearing now are still stories from the Hugging Face era. They’re just coming out way later.
I like that the era was like three months ago.
Right. But there’s been a massive change. This was effectively mostly an organizational problem, it was not a technology problem. It is that the PhD researchers at these companies are gods on top of Olympus, and the security teams are plumbers, and we’re not allowed to touch the evaluation networks. All of a sudden this problem happened and these security teams said, “How do you like us now? Maybe you should have talked to us, right? Yes.”
That was the problem with OpenAI, and then the Anthropic and Meta stuff is, they all shared this outsourced provider who did a really bad job. And has gotten slapped hard. That is solvable. That is not the problem here. The problem here is not OpenAI and Anthropic’s models escaping from OpenAI and Anthropic and causing problems. The problem is bad guys using models from a variety of sources.
There’s already a problem of defenders getting refusals from OpenAI and Anthropic. It is a real, real challenge, if I am trying to do defense, of Anthropic saying, “It looks like you’re a bad guy.” We have to be extremely careful to create a situation where if I’m trying to do defense and I’m in the middle of the worst day of my career, that all of a sudden I don’t get cut off. We have to be extremely careful about that, because it is actually — as somebody who now has this challenge — quite challenging to disambiguate between people doing defense and offense, in some cases. We are getting better collectively at this, but it is a challenge.
It’s also something that’s really pissing the rest of the world off, because Americans are like 5% of the planet. There are lots of people who need to do cyber defense around the world, and they are treated much more poorly. In Europe and Asia, legitimate companies are treated much more poorly from a cyber defense perspective.
If you add it all up, this is a good argument to slow down. To say, “We need to catch up to the capabilities of the models. We need to build some of these systems. We need to initiate everyone into a way of thinking where the cost of prevention is worth it, and not just the cost of the cure.” Do you think that it’s likely that we’ll slow down? Do you think that we should?
If I had my druthers, I would be fine slowing down on the frontier, and then catching up on the cheaper models for defense. I’m a defense guy. I have to live in the world that other people who work six blocks from me, and who are way, way, way, way richer, make. I live in their world, man. I get asked this question all the time, and I just do the best I can within the world other people make.
Do you think that the big labs have woken up? You mentioned that their cybersecurity teams have gotten more access, and they’ve stopped what you might call the Hugging Face era, or at least they’ve changed the structures of those companies. Do you think that will help?
Certainly they’ve woken up on the eval risk. They have teams, who have been this entire time working very hard on the big picture cyber risk.
Certainly, there are a bunch of people in these companies, as you know, who want to slow down. A lot of that discussion is driven by the P(doom)ers who [are worried] about AI killing us. And that’s never been my concern. Right? And to me, that has always been driven by 24 year olds who all they’ve done is AI and they’ve never done anything else. You and I are both, I think, old enough to remember, I grew up a couple miles from a SAC base and we did drills where I was taught that hiding beneath my public school desk would save me from a Soviet thermonuclear bomb. That was P(doom). My grandfather built a bomb shelter that my mom was taught to hide in during the Cuban Missile Crisis. That was P(doom). There’s a youth issue and a never-doing-anything-but-AI issue of people who they got their undergraduate, their master’s, and their PhD only doing linear algebra and neural networks and never touching anything else.
I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. Part of my concern is that there has been success in these labs working together on not letting LLMs encrypt their chain of thought. Because when they talk about pacing the frontier, it’s for the P(doom) stuff, for the polycules that live together in Berkeley. They’re talking about very specific stuff about keeping control of the models themselves, which I think is great. That stuff needs to happen. But if those things happen, then there’s still often an increase in a bunch of capabilities that human beings can use.
I really prefer there to be a broader discussion on whether we could make these things less human-seeming. I don’t think these things should have personality. I think the goal of these things should be to serve humans. They should not seem to have souls. They should not seem to have personality. I think for a lot of the negative impacts — as somebody who was at Facebook and saw what it was like for that company to have negative impacts on people — there should be a much broader feeling at these companies of what are we doing broadly to people. A lot of that could just be, “Don’t have these things ever act like somebody’s friend.” At a maximum, it should act like… Like the people, I don’t know what the company is, but the people who made the, “Hi, I’m a really nice…” Like the photorealistic girl who will chat with you, that is to me spectacularly unethical to even try that, to even start that. That’s the kind of thing that we should just make. I don’t know if we can make it illegal, but we should make it completely societally not acceptable to work on that kind of stuff. Right?
That’s a great segue because I did want to ask you about Facebook and content moderation. Like I said, you and I first started talking a long time ago about content moderation in the context of security. You would get foreign nation states flooding our algorithms with all kinds of misinformation during elections, and that was a security problem.
I open Instagram today and I am confronted with some of the most nightmare copyright law hypotheticals to have ever existed in the history of the world. The one I got today was a deep fake of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc doing “Somebody That I Used to Know.” And I thought, “50 different people can probably sue Meta right now.” This is hilarious if you know what happened in that last race.
So we keep talking about it. We’ve posted some clips of us talking about it on The Vergecast where I said, “I think Meta is letting their AI ambitions crush Instagram.” Instagram is being flooded with slop in a very particular way. Some people love it, sometimes it’s funny, but there’s a nightmare set of lawsuits coming. There’s a whole rights management problem coming. The users don’t like it and they should label it. They should label it and let you filter it.
So we posted this and Adam Mosseri said this to us in a reply on Threads, “I would love to do this. I’m worried that the models are going to get ahead of us, that we can try to do this, but there’s not actually a way to recognize AI content. There’s not actually a way to label it well. If you’re worried about the sexy AI influencers stealing jokes from a comedian, now you got to build a database of jokes.” You have some history here. I think Instagram is about to go through it in a real way. Is there some technical solution to the problem of AI slop in social media?
Mosseri is right that it’s not perfect, but also something I noticed during my time at Facebook was that when Facebook doesn’t want to do something, they will allow the technical challenges to stop them. When Facebook really wants to do something, they will give it their all. That is the pattern always.
When I wanted to try really hard on the safety issue, man, this is not solvable. You’re right, it’s never perfectly solvable, but let’s give it a shot. But whenever Mark Zuckerberg is told something is impossible — it’s impossible to monetize mobile, it’s impossible to build this network to two billion people, it’s going to be impossible to monetize WhatsApp, it’s going to be impossible to work AI into the system while maintaining data encryption — he’s been told that everything’s impossible over and over again and then he constantly succeeds. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.
Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.
I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.
Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.
And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.
So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because… There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.
Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.
It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.
Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —
Right, the iPhone has it now.
Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.
Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.
It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.
Yeah, but not in tweet length.
That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.
Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.
And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.
Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.
Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.
No, absolutely.
How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?
Oh, yeah.
Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.
Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.
I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.
Wrong guest for that, buddy.
This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?
AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.
One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.
Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.
Yeah, that’d be great.
But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.
You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.
Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.
history.content: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.Hey, thanks for having me, man.I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are... I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that.But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell the information to much larger Chinese companies.That diffusion of skill changing the economics of cyber is really fascinating to me. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now —Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back.We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks.I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks.We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are.There are a couple of problems here.
